title: Was Sunomata Castle Really Built in One Night?
description:
Legend says Kinoshita Tōkichirō (later Toyotomi Hideyoshi) built Oda Nobunaga a castle at Sunomata in a single night. This episode opens the story layer by layer, in the order the books appeared.

Ōta Gyūichi's Shinchō Kōki mentions Sunomata in its opening volume only in Eiroku 4 (1561): Nobunaga orders the strongpoint made secure and pulls out within a month; in the edition we found, the opening volume has no "Tōkichirō." The earliest account we found of Hideyoshi building a castle in Mino is Oze Hoan's Taikōki (preface 1625): work starts on the 5th of the 9th month, Eiroku 9, and is largely done by the 7th or 8th, three or four days; that chapter names no place. The Mino no Kuni Shokyūki gives Eiroku 5 and "within days"; only the Ehon Taikōki, published from 1797, makes it "one night," with board walls covered in white paper and painted loopholes. In the Meiji era, Tanaka Yoshinari in his lectures and Watanabe Yosuke in his 1905 Waseda lecture notes adopted Hoan's Eiroku 9 (October 1566, Julian). The Bukō Yawa, published in 1987, is disputed: Fujimoto Masayuki, Suzuki Masaya, Hattori Hideo and others question it, while Miki Seiichirō, Owada Tetsuo and others hold it is no forgery; this episode does not rule. Ōgaki City itself says its museum (1991) was given "the look of a castle keep."

Verdict: "one night" is filed; whether Hideyoshi built at Sunomata stays open. The Sōkenki, other 18th-century war chronicles and contemporary documents were not opened this time. Narration dates use the old lunar calendar; "we think" is this channel's view.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters, not likenesses; modern researchers and battles are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-20

**castle wall?**
thumbnail.sub: A night from the Kansei era

sm101.text: Kansei 9: an Osaka press prints an illustrated novel, the Ehon Taikōki.

sm102.text: Workers haul logs by night to Sunomata, then spelled otherwise.

sm103.text: Beams go up by their marks; the board walls get white paper;

sm104.text: then painters draw arrow slits and gun ports on it.

sm105.text: At dawn, Mino soldiers look across from afar:

sm106.text: a long wall has suddenly appeared.

sm107.text: They say: this must be tengu work.

sm109.text: Nobunaga's retainer wrote of Sunomata too. Is Tōkichirō in those lines?

sm110.text: 20-odd years after Hideyoshi died, a biography gave it a schedule.

sm111.text: In the Meiji era, a Tokyo Imperial professor gave it a year.

sm112.text: Sunomata really has a castle today; the city added a note about it.

sm113.text: Was that castle really built in one night?

sm201.text: That retainer was Ōta Gyūichi; his Shinchō Kōki mentions Sunomata about two hundred years before that novel.

sm202.text: Dictionaries date the book to around Keichō 3; its opening volume covers Nobunaga before he entered Kyoto.

sm203.text: In early 5th month, Eiroku 4, Nobunaga crossed two great rivers into western Mino.

sm204.text: Sunomata was a Saitō base; that same month, the enemy marched from it.

sm205.text: Nobunaga had its defenses secured and camped there.

sm206.text: "Secured," not newly built; and it doesn't say by whom.

sm208.text: On the morning of the 24th, 5th month, he came back; then

sm209.text: he abandoned Sunomata, less than a month in all.

sm210.text: In this record, it's Nobunaga himself who comes and goes.

sm211.text: And the Tōkichirō we asked about?

sm212.text: In the edition we read, "Tōkichirō" never appears in the opening volume.

sm213.text: He first appears here in the 9th month of Eiroku 11, attacking Mount Mitsukuri.

sm214.text: So who first wrote the story of Tōkichirō building Nobunaga a castle?

sm301.text: The earliest we found is Oze Hoan's Taikōki, preface dated Kan'ei 2.

sm302.text: It says Nobunaga wanted a stronghold across the river and asked who would lead;

sm303.text: no one would cross over and live on enemy ground.

sm304.text: But Tōkichirō stepped up: Owari's villages were full of good fighters.

sm305.text: Name by name they were listed, over 1,200 men;

sm306.text: on the list was one Hachisuka Koroku.

sm307.text: That timetable starts on the 5th day of the 7th month, Eiroku 9:

sm308.text: ten barracks, ten towers, 2,000 ken of wall, 50,000 stakes, all ready by the 20th of the 8th month.

sm309.text: Publicly, the book says, it was to be built in Ise;

sm310.text: the men split in three: one to hold the enemy, two to build.

sm311.text: How to get all that timber across?

sm312.text: 9th month, day 1: the timber lay piled by the river like a hill;

sm313.text: skilled river villagers lashed it into rafts upstream and floated it down.

sm314.text: On the 4th they met at Komakiyama; before dawn on the 5th they crossed and put up a palisade.

sm315.text: How many days did it take?

sm316.text: By the 7th and 8th, the castle was largely complete.

sm317.text: Three or four days from the start; not one night.

sm318.text: It does mention a night: walls and towers up, plastered that night.

sm319.text: A night of plastering, not of castle-building.

sm320.text: Tōkichirō was left to hold it with a garrison.

sm321.text: The odd part is where: the chapter only says the army "reached Mino," never Sunomata.

sm322.text: Yet a page earlier, he had written that very name.

sm323.text: The name printed there, in other characters, is Sunomata.

sm324.text: Stranger still, the book's opening notes name that same Ōta Gyūichi.

sm325.text: Hoan says his book builds on Gyūichi's record,

sm326.text: and that Gyūichi, honest by nature, took whatever he heard as true.

sm327.text: He admits he didn't check much himself.

sm328.text: So in which book were "Sunomata" and "Tōkichirō" first joined?

sm401.text: Of the books we opened, it's an Edo-period history of Mino: the Mino no Kuni Shokyūki.

sm402.text: Author unknown; even its date is a guess.

sm403.text: It puts the castle in Eiroku 5:

sm404.text: Sakuma is sent and driven back; then Shibata, whose stone and timber get thrown out.

sm405.text: Third, it goes to Kinoshita Tōkichirō Hideyoshi.

sm406.text: Work began the night of the 27th, 5th month;

sm407.text: in a few days the fort stood; Hideyoshi became lord of Sunomata.

sm408.text: Hoan said three or four days, this says a few days; so where does "one night" come from?

sm409.text: Remember that Osaka illustrated novel? It too starts in Eiroku 5.

sm410.text: Sakuma, with 5,000 laborers and a 20-day limit, fails; Shibata takes over and fails too.

sm411.text: Then Tōkichirō says: no Oda laborers, no bamboo or timber cut in Owari,

sm412.text: the Sunomata fort, fully built within seven days.

sm413.text: How would he pull that off?

sm414.text: He has 1,000 laborers in Owari, on the north bank, cut beams to plan;

sm415.text: Koroku's men dig a moat on the Mino bank, south, and make the base of its earth.

sm416.text: Yet by the end, the seven days he boasted of have become one night.

sm417.text: Of the books we opened, this is the first to say "one night."

sm418.text: Some say it comes from an earlier war chronicle, the Sōkenki; we didn't open that one.

sm419.text: The first edition illustrated it: one picture shows workers on ladders by lantern;

sm420.text: the other is odder: a castle with stone walls and towers.

sm421.text: We think that white paper wall looks more like a stage set.

sm422.text: Yet today's dictionaries and Ōgaki City's website all say 1566: Hoan's year.

sm423.text: Edo books say Eiroku 5 or Eiroku 9; so who chose this year?

sm501.text: The Tokyo professor from the opening: Tanaka Yoshinari.

sm502.text: In lectures, per Hoan's Taikōki and the Hideyoshi Fu, he set the castle in that year.

sm503.text: In 1905, Watanabe Yosuke's Waseda lecture notes put it more plainly:

sm504.text: "Under Dr. Tanaka's guidance, set at Eiroku 9, 9th month; all earlier views rejected."

sm505.text: And what year did earlier views give?

sm506.text: Eiroku 4; earlier histories all said so, he wrote.

sm508.text: Old histories read it as Tōkichirō building that year.

sm509.text: In 1916, Watanabe put this into his general history, Azuchi-Momoyama Jidaishi.

sm510.text: In 1987, papers kept by an old Aichi family were published: the Bukō Yawa.

sm511.text: Where did these papers come from?

sm512.text: Reportedly, they were found when the 1959 Isewan Typhoon flooded a storehouse.

sm513.text: It tells how Sunomata was built in minute detail.

sm514.text: Ōgaki City's website says these papers gradually revealed the full picture.

sm515.text: But when were these papers written?

sm516.text: One researcher found the place name Tomika;

sm517.text: a name that only arose with a merger in Shōwa 29.

sm518.text: Another saw the original in 2000 and judged it an Edo-period copy, not a forgery.

sm519.text: The debate has run over thirty years.

sm520.text: In 1991, on the Sunomata castle site, modeled on Ōgaki Castle, a reinforced-concrete keep went up.

sm521.text: And the exhibits inside rely on exactly these papers.

sm522.text: The note we mentioned is on Ōgaki City's website:

sm523.text: not a fort of that era, but built in a keep's image.

sm524.text: Even "built in one night" the city marks "reportedly."

sm525.text: We think that honest phrase is worth more of a look than the keep.

sm526.text: Remember the Mino soldiers who cried tengu? Their night was written 170 years after Hoan.

sm527.text: The "one night" case: filed. What Hideyoshi built at Sunomata: still open.

sm528.text: First heard of the one-night castle in manga, a game, or a textbook?

sm529.text: We tell only what records show. Subscribe to open the files with us.
